title: The foundation of foundations
hookLine: the code opens with knowing that there is a first Being
carry: first, know there is a first being

lines: THE ONE UNDER ALL THE OTHERS.
cards: Yesod. In Hebrew, a foundation, the part of a building nobody looks at. Walls get painted.
Windows get admired. The foundation sits under the soil, and if it shifts, the whole house cracks. Now double the word.
Not a foundation, but the foundation of foundations, the one under all the others. That is how Maimonides opens his entire code of Jewish law: with one sentence about what everything else stands on.

teach.h: TO KNOW, NOT ONLY TO FEEL.
teach.b: Here is the sentence, in plain English: the foundation of foundations and the pillar of wisdom is to know that there is a First Being, and that it brings every other thing into being. First, the verb.
Maimonides says to know. Not to feel, not to hope, not simply to accept.
For him this is something the mind works at, the way it works at geometry, and the following chapters lead the reader through reasoning, not only through faith. Second, what kind of Being.
If you could imagine it did not exist, he goes on, nothing else could exist. Imagine everything else gone, and it alone would still be.
Everything leans on it. It leans on nothing. Third, the commandment.

teach.h: I AM THE LORD THY GOD.
teach.b: Knowing this, he says, is a commandment, and he points to the opening words of the Ten Commandments: "I am the LORD thy God." For him, that line is the first thing the Torah asks a person to know.
Last week, Crescas asked whether belief in God can be commanded at all. Here is the view he was answering. Fourth, a detail some readers love.
In Hebrew the opening runs yesod ha-yesodot ve-amud ha-chochmot. Take the first letter of each word: yud, heh, vav, heh. Together they spell the name of God written with those letters.
Some see a signature hidden in the cornerstone. Others call it a lovely coincidence.

teach.h: THE NAME INSIDE THE FIRST SENTENCE.
teach.b: Either way, the code's first sentence carries the name inside it.

how: Students of the Mishneh Torah often begin with this opening halakhah, and some learn it by heart in Hebrew. Jews who study Maimonides' code read these chapters as a guide to knowing God through careful thought.

games.why: he opens with knowing there is a First Being, the foundation of foundations, and ties it to "I am the LORD thy God."

practice: Feel what's holding you up: the chair, the floor under the chair, the building under the floor, the earth under the building.
Let your attention go down layer by layer, and notice that you didn't build any of it, and it holds you anyway.
If you pray, rest with the words "I am the LORD thy God"; if you don't, simply stay with the feeling of being held from below.
